title: Scanless quantum Fourier-transform mid-infrared spectroscopy for solids and surface analysis
authors: Paul Gattinger, Michela Conti, Franziska Dietz, Andrei N. Halangescu Moldovan, Andreas W. Schell, Markus Brandstetter, Ivan Zorin
abstract: Quantum infrared (IR) spectroscopy is a novel technique based on nonlinear interferometry and quantum sensing with undetected photons. In this approach, spectrally far-separated correlated photon pairs are used for detection and probing, respectively. Hence, the probing wavelength domain (mid-IR) is substantially different from the detection spectral range (near-IR), which enables shot-noise-limited and cost-effective sensing schemes attractive for applied metrology. In this paper, we implement and employ a custom-built scanless quantum Fourier-transform mid-IR (sQFTIR) microspectrometer for chemical characterization and analysis of solids and interfaces. The sQFTIR system employs spectral-domain acquisition, without the need to scan the optical delay. This results in enhanced sensitivity and short measurement times and therefore enables rapid spectral acquisitions in 100~ms spanning a spectral band from 3000 cm$^{-1}$ - 2400 cm$^{-1}$. The capabilities of our approach are demonstrated for hyperspectral mid-IR imaging of dried pharmaceuticals (insulin on a gold surface) and investigation of a security feature on a banknote. Furthermore, we demonstrate hyperspectral imaging and spectroscopy through a turbid ceramic medium.
summary: This paper introduces and validates a scanless quantum Fourier-transform mid-IR (sQFTIR) microspectrometer. By using quantum sensing with correlated photon pairs, it achieves rapid, shot-noise-limited spectral measurements. The technique is demonstrated to be highly effective for non-destructive chemical analysis of diverse materials, including pharmaceuticals and security features.
main_problem: Developing a novel, rapid, and sensitive technique for chemical characterization and analysis of solids and interfaces using mid-infrared (mid-IR) spectroscopy.
main_result: The custom-built scanless quantum Fourier-transform mid-IR (sQFTIR) system successfully demonstrated hyperspectral imaging of pharmaceuticals, banknote security features, and polymer identification through turbid media.
method: The technique utilizes quantum infrared spectroscopy based on nonlinear interferometry, employing correlated photon pairs generated via SPDC to achieve spectral-domain acquisition without mechanical scanning.
model_or_system: The system is a sQFTIR microspectrometer using a double-pass configuration with a periodically poled nonlinear crystal (ppKTP). It measures the interference of joint generation probabilities to infer the mid-IR spectrum from near-IR signal photons.
key_observables: Absorbance spectra in the functional group region ($3000 	ext{ cm}^{-1} – 2400 	ext{ cm}^{-1}$), fringe visibility, and spectral images.
important_parameters: Measurement speed of 100 ms, spectral range of $3000 	ext{ cm}^{-1} – 2400 	ext{ cm}^{-1}$, and spatial resolution on the tens-of-micrometer scale.
main_assumptions: The technique assumes operation in the low-gain regime where difference frequency generation can be neglected.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the experimental setup (Michelson-type interferometer) and show hyperspectral imaging results for dried insulin on gold, a banknote security feature, and polymer identification through a turbid ceramic medium.
paper_structure: The paper details the underlying quantum principles of the sQFTIR setup, describes the spectral-domain acquisition and Fourier transform processing, and then demonstrates the technique's capabilities through multiple applied examples.
why_interesting: The core physics relies heavily on quantum optics, specifically nonlinear frequency conversion (SPDC) and quantum sensing principles, making it highly relevant to quantum optics and open quantum systems.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Experimental setup: the sQFTIR hyperspectral imaging system based on a nonlinear interferometer with a Michelson topology. A pump beam (660 nm continuous-wave laser) is sent into the system through a cold mirror (CM) and focused into a ppKTP crystal type-0 phase-matched for non-degenerate SPDC. In the first pump-pass, the nonlinear crystal produces idler-signal photon pairs through SPDC. The idler, signal and pump beams are collimated by an off-axis parabolic mirror (OAPM) and sent to a dichroic mirror (DM) that reflects pump and signal photons while transmitting the idler.
